h1: AIP diet and food labels: what to scan for in every ingredient list.
metaTitle: AIP food scanner: find compliant products instantly — Nouri
metaDescription: Following AIP? Nouri scans food labels against your diet automatically — flags non-compliant ingredients before they reach your cart. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
The Autoimmune Protocol, commonly known as AIP, is a structured elimination diet designed to reduce inflammation and support gut integrity in people managing autoimmune conditions. The protocol removes food groups and compounds thought to increase intestinal permeability or stimulate immune activity. The elimination phase restricts grains, legumes, dairy, eggs, nightshade vegetables and spices, nuts, seeds, seed-based oils, seed spices, alcohol, food additives, and refined sugars. The rationale is that removing these inputs gives the immune system and gut lining an opportunity to stabilize before a structured reintroduction phase begins.

On food labels, AIP compliance requires checking for a wide range of excluded items that appear under multiple names. Nightshade-derived additives include paprika, cayenne, chili powder, red pepper flakes, and "spices" as a catch-all term — which may legally contain ground nightshade peppers. Seed-based oils such as sunflower, safflower, canola, sesame, and corn oil are excluded. Legume derivatives including soy lecithin, carob, and pea protein are non-compliant. Additives such as carrageenan, xanthan gum, guar gum, and emulsifiers are excluded in the elimination phase. Many of these appear in products marketed as "natural," "organic," or "clean," which can create a false sense of compliance.

Foods most likely to require scrutiny on AIP: packaged broths and stocks, sauces and marinades, canned goods with added seasoning, plant-based meat substitutes, gluten-free baked goods, condiments, and dairy alternatives.

AIP label reading is one of the most demanding dietary protocols to maintain manually because the exclusion list is long and the hidden names are numerous — particularly for seed spices inside "spices" catch-alls and additive gums in otherwise clean-looking products. h1: FODMAP diet and food labels: what to scan for in every ingredient list.
metaTitle: FODMAP food scanner: find compliant products instantly — Nouri
metaDescription: Following FODMAP? Nouri scans food labels against your diet automatically — flags non-compliant ingredients before they reach your cart. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
The low-FODMAP diet is an evidence-based dietary intervention developed at Monash University in Australia, primarily used for managing irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and other functional gut disorders. FODMAP is an acronym for Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides, and Polyols — a group of short-chain carbohydrates and sugar alcohols that are poorly absorbed in the small intestine and fermented by gut bacteria, producing gas and triggering symptoms in sensitive individuals. The protocol involves a structured three-phase approach: elimination, reintroduction, and personalization.

On food labels, high-FODMAP ingredients to watch for include: fructose in excess of glucose (found in high-fructose corn syrup, fruit juice concentrates, honey, and agave), lactose (in milk, soft cheeses, and ice cream), fructooligosaccharides (FOS) and inulin (added prebiotic fibers in many "gut health" products), wheat and rye in large quantities, garlic and onion derivatives (including garlic powder, onion powder, and "natural flavors" which may contain these), polyols such as sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol, erythritol, and maltitol (common in sugar-free and diet products), and legumes including chickpeas, lentils, and kidney beans. Serving size is important in FODMAP — some ingredients are low-FODMAP at small quantities but high-FODMAP at larger ones.

Foods most likely to require scrutiny on FODMAP: sugar-free and diet products (polyols), prebiotic-enriched yogurts and cereals, garlic-seasoned snacks, wheat-based products, fruit juice beverages, protein bars with chicory root fiber.

FODMAP label reading is complicated by the fact that high-FODMAP ingredients appear frequently in foods marketed for gut health — prebiotic inulin in yogurt, chicory root in fiber bars — making those products traps for people managing IBS. h1: NOVA-4-Free diet and food labels: what to scan for in every ingredient list.
metaTitle: NOVA-4-Free food scanner: find compliant products instantly — Nouri
metaDescription: Following NOVA-4-Free? Nouri scans food labels against your diet automatically — flags non-compliant ingredients before they reach your cart. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
The NOVA food classification system, developed by researchers at the University of Sao Paulo, categorizes foods into four groups based on the extent and purpose of industrial processing. NOVA 4 — the Ultra-Processed Foods category — includes products that are formulated largely from industrial ingredients, additives, and substances derived from food with little or no whole food content. A NOVA-4-free approach involves avoiding NOVA 4 products in favor of foods in groups 1 through 3: unprocessed or minimally processed foods (group 1), processed culinary ingredients (group 2), and processed foods (group 3 — products with a small number of added ingredients like salt or sugar to preserve or enhance whole foods).

On food labels, NOVA 4 classification markers include the presence of additives that serve cosmetic or sensory functions rather than preservation: artificial flavors, artificial colors, synthetic sweeteners (aspartame, sucralose, acesulfame-K), thickeners and stabilizers (xanthan gum, carrageenan, guar gum), emulsifiers (soy lecithin, mono- and diglycerides, polysorbate 80), flavor enhancers (monosodium glutamate, autolyzed yeast extract), and hydrogenated oils. A useful heuristic: if the ingredient list contains items a home cook would not use in a kitchen, the product is likely NOVA 4. Ingredient count alone is not determinative — a product with five ingredients that include polysorbate 80 is NOVA 4; a product with twelve whole-food ingredients is NOVA 3.

Foods most likely to be NOVA 4: packaged snack foods, flavored chips, flavored breakfast cereals, meal-replacement products, flavored drinks, margarine, most fast food items, packaged baked goods, protein bars.

NOVA 4 identification by label reading requires pattern-recognition across a wide range of additive classes, which is difficult to do quickly in a supermarket. Nouri analyzes the ingredient list and assigns a processing level assessment to flag NOVA 4 products before they reach your cart.
